cases.title: The Afternoon Collapse
cases.summary: A vigorous plant looks fine after lights-on, then repeatedly loses turgor late in the light period.
symptoms: Leaves hang softly instead of clawing
Top growth recovers quickly after irrigation
No standing runoff or sour odor

inspections.label: Lift the container
inspections.result: The root ball is much lighter than comparable plants at the same point in the cycle.

inspections.label: Check media moisture
inspections.result: The upper and middle root zone are both dry; moisture is not lingering deep in the container.

inspections.label: Inspect leaf posture
inspections.result: Petiole and blade both droop softly, with no dark clawing at the tips.

inspections.label: Review irrigation timing
inspections.result: The last irrigation interval was longer than the recent plant demand pattern.

cases.explanation: The strongest pattern is a root ball that has dried beyond the plant's current demand. The key clue is rapid recovery after irrigation combined with a genuinely light, dry container.

cases.title: The Never-Dry Pot
cases.summary: A plant remains limp for days even though the surface looks moist and irrigation has been frequent.
symptoms: Lower leaves yellow slowly
Growth rate has stalled
Media remains wet between irrigations

inspections.label: Lift the container
inspections.result: The container is still heavy long after the previous irrigation.

inspections.label: Probe media moisture
inspections.result: Moisture remains high through most of the root zone rather than only near the surface.

inspections.label: Review irrigation log
inspections.result: Irrigations have been scheduled by the clock even when the container had not dried back.

inspections.label: Inspect accessible roots
inspections.result: Visible roots look pale and stressed, but there is no evidence of a dry root ball.

cases.explanation: Persistent saturation and a heavy container point to excess irrigation frequency. The broad lesson is to match irrigation timing to root-zone conditions rather than a rigid clock.

cases.title: The Suffocating Bench
cases.summary: Plants in one bench are slowing down despite adequate moisture and otherwise stable room conditions.
symptoms: Roots are slow to colonize the lower pot
Leaves appear dull and slightly drooped
Problem is worst in containers with poor drainage

inspections.label: Inspect drainage
inspections.result: Drain holes clear slowly and the lower media remains saturated well after the upper zone begins drying.

inspections.label: Inspect root distribution
inspections.result: Most healthy roots are concentrated near the upper, better-aerated portion of the container.

inspections.label: Compare media structure
inspections.result: Affected pots are noticeably denser and less porous than the healthy control pots.

inspections.label: Check root-zone temperature
inspections.result: Root-zone temperature is normal, so chilling is not the strongest explanation.

cases.explanation: The pattern is low oxygen availability in a dense, persistently wet root zone. Saturation may contribute, but the diagnostic focus is the poor air-water balance around the roots.

cases.title: The Fast-Drying Canopy
cases.summary: The room is warm and very dry. Plants transpire hard and leaf edges begin to curl upward during peak light.
symptoms: Leaf edges taco upward
Containers dry much faster than last week
Symptoms intensify during the hottest hours

inspections.label: Review temperature and RH
inspections.result: The temperature/RH combination produces a substantially drier air demand than the room had previously.

inspections.label: Compare symptom timing
inspections.result: Curling peaks when temperature rises and RH falls, then eases after the environment moderates.

inspections.label: Compare by light intensity
inspections.result: Plants at similar intensity but in a more humid zone show less stress.

inspections.label: Check root-zone moisture
inspections.result: The media is drying quickly, but several plants show stress before the root zone is fully dry.

cases.explanation: The strongest common driver is excessive atmospheric drying demand. High VPD can increase transpiration pressure even before the root zone is completely dry.

cases.title: The Damp Corner
cases.summary: One corner of the room stays humid and still while the rest of the canopy looks normal.
symptoms: Leaf surfaces stay soft and slow to dry
Growth feels less vigorous in the corner
Issue maps to a humid microclimate

inspections.label: Move a sensor into the canopy
inspections.result: Canopy-level RH in the affected pocket is much higher than the room-average sensor reports.

inspections.label: Check air movement
inspections.result: Leaves barely move in the affected corner while adjacent zones have visible circulation.

inspections.label: Compare light level
inspections.result: Light level is similar to nearby healthy plants, making low light a weaker fit.

inspections.label: Compare pot weight
inspections.result: Affected and healthy containers have similar moisture status.

cases.explanation: A localized humid, stagnant microclimate is the defining pattern. The lesson is to diagnose conditions at canopy level rather than relying only on a room-average reading.

cases.title: The Pale Summit
cases.summary: Only the tallest tops directly under the fixture become pale and stressed after the light was lowered.
symptoms: Paling is concentrated at the highest tops
Leaf edges near the fixture curl upward
Lower canopy remains normally colored

inspections.label: Map symptoms against fixture position
inspections.result: The strongest bleaching forms a clear hotspot directly under the most intense part of the fixture.

inspections.label: Review recent changes
inspections.result: Symptoms began shortly after the fixture height was reduced.

inspections.label: Inspect lower leaves
inspections.result: Lower and shaded leaves remain healthy rather than showing a whole-plant nutrient pattern.

inspections.label: Check room climate
inspections.result: Temperature and RH are stable enough that atmospheric stress alone does not explain the hotspot pattern.

cases.explanation: A top-only hotspot that follows a recent intensity increase strongly supports excess light stress. Spatial pattern is often more useful than a single leaf color.

cases.title: The Long Internodes
cases.summary: A group of young plants is stretching, leaning, and making wide internodes despite otherwise healthy color.
symptoms: Long internodes
Thin stems lean toward the brightest side
Leaf color remains generally healthy

inspections.label: Compare light intensity
inspections.result: The affected tray is receiving substantially less light than the neighboring healthy tray.

inspections.label: Observe plant direction
inspections.result: Stems consistently lean toward the brighter edge of the room.

inspections.label: Compare leaf color
inspections.result: Leaves are not showing the progressive lower-leaf yellowing expected from a strong nitrogen shortage.

inspections.label: Check root-zone temperature
inspections.result: The root zone is within the same range as the healthy tray.

cases.explanation: Stretch plus directional leaning and confirmed low intensity point to insufficient light. The pattern is architectural, not simply a color symptom.

cases.title: The Mixed Deficiency Look
cases.summary: Several nutrient-like symptoms appear at once even though the feed recipe has not changed and reservoir strength looks normal.
symptoms: Interveinal paling on some leaves
Slow new growth
Multiple deficiency-like patterns appear together

inspections.label: Check root-zone pH trend
inspections.result: Recent root-zone readings have drifted well outside the grower's usual target range.

inspections.label: Verify fresh input
inspections.result: Fresh input strength is consistent with the established recipe rather than obviously underfed.

inspections.label: Compare symptom pattern
inspections.result: The symptoms do not follow one clean nutrient-deficiency progression; several availability patterns overlap.

inspections.label: Check concentration trend
inspections.result: Concentration has not risen enough to make salt accumulation the primary signal.

cases.explanation: When several availability-like symptoms appear together, verify root-zone conditions before adding more nutrients. Here, the strongest evidence is the documented pH drift.

cases.title: The Rising Concentration
cases.summary: Plants receive the same feed strength as before, but the root zone is getting progressively more concentrated and leaf tips are burning.
symptoms: Burnt leaf tips
Darkening margins on older leaves
Root-zone concentration trend keeps rising

inspections.label: Review EC trend
inspections.result: Root-zone or runoff concentration has climbed across several irrigations instead of returning toward baseline.

inspections.label: Inspect media surface
inspections.result: A light mineral crust is visible around high-evaporation areas of the container.

inspections.label: Check fresh solution
inspections.result: Fresh input is not unusually strong, so the concentration increase is occurring in the root zone.

inspections.label: Inspect leaf posture
inspections.result: Leaves do not show the uniform dark-green clawing expected from excess nitrogen as the main issue.

cases.explanation: The decisive clue is a rising root-zone concentration over time despite stable input. That accumulation pattern is more informative than tip burn alone.

cases.title: The Fading Lower Deck
cases.summary: Older lower leaves are gradually paling while newer growth stays greener and the root zone is otherwise behaving normally.
symptoms: Yellowing begins on older lower leaves
New growth remains comparatively green
No tip burn or severe clawing

inspections.label: Trace symptom progression
inspections.result: The paling consistently begins on older leaves and moves upward over time.

inspections.label: Check root-zone conditions
inspections.result: Moisture rhythm and pH trend are stable enough that root dysfunction is a weaker explanation.

inspections.label: Compare canopy positions
inspections.result: Lower leaves fade even where light exposure differs, so simple shading does not fully explain the pattern.

inspections.label: Review nutrition history
inspections.result: The crop has recently increased growth rate without a corresponding change in nitrogen supply.

cases.explanation: A mobile-nutrient pattern beginning on older leaves, paired with otherwise stable root-zone conditions, supports a nitrogen shortage in this game case.

cases.title: The Dark Hook
cases.summary: Plants are very dark green and leaf tips hook downward even though the media is not waterlogged.
symptoms: Unusually dark foliage
Downward clawing at leaf tips
New growth is slower and softer

inspections.label: Compare foliage color
inspections.result: Affected plants are noticeably darker than healthy reference plants of the same cultivar and age.

inspections.label: Check container moisture
inspections.result: Containers are drying normally and are not persistently saturated.

inspections.label: Review recent feed changes
inspections.result: Nitrogen-containing inputs were increased shortly before the dark clawing appeared.

inspections.label: Review EC trend
inspections.result: Overall concentration is elevated only modestly; the strongest unique clue is the nitrogen-heavy change plus dark clawing.

cases.explanation: Dark green foliage plus downward tip clawing after a nitrogen-heavy change supports excess nitrogen more strongly than simple overwatering in this case.

cases.title: The Chilled Root Zone
cases.summary: A floor-level tray grows slowly each morning even though the room air warms quickly after lights-on.
environment: Containers sit on a cold slab
symptoms: Morning growth is sluggish
Root zone warms hours after room air
Problem is strongest on floor-level containers

inspections.label: Measure root-zone temperature
inspections.result: The media is much colder than the room air during the first hours after lights-on.

inspections.label: Compare elevated containers
inspections.result: Plants raised off the slab maintain warmer media and are growing faster under the same light.

inspections.label: Inspect drainage
inspections.result: Drainage is acceptable, so persistent saturation is not the primary difference between trays.

inspections.label: Compare light level
inspections.result: Light intensity is similar across the affected and healthy trays.

cases.explanation: The spatial and timing pattern tracks cold media rather than room air. Root-zone temperature can differ substantially from the headline room temperature.
